pages.text: Lockerbie bombing suspect seized from Libya in 'cloak and dagger' operation Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Lockerbie bombing suspect seized from Libya in 'cloak and dagger' operation 13 October 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google David Cowan Scotland home affairs correspondent Media outlet Libyan Review broadcast footage of Abu Agila Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi in a US prison A Lockerbie bombing suspect has claimed he was illegally removed from Libya to stand trial in the United States after "a cloak and dagger operation conducted in the dead of night". Abu Agila Mohammad Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi has alleged he was abducted by armed men and handed over "hooded and bound" to FBI agents, who had a plane waiting to fly him out of the country. Al-Marimi, also known as Mas'ud, has denied building and priming the bomb that brought down Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie on 21 December 1988, killing 270 people. The Libyan argues he was the victim of an unlawful rendition and has asked a judge in Washington DC to throw the case out of court. In response, the US Department of Justice said, under American law, the manner of his removal should not stop his thrice-postponed trial from finally getting underway in January. Al-Marimi's version of what happened is detailed for the first time in papers lodged with the court by his legal team. pages.text: Los Mirlos: Tiny Desk Concert : NPR Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player Los Mirlos: Tiny Desk Concert For more than 50 years, Los Mirlos has cultivated its own Peruvian twist on cumbia, featuring reverb-heavy, surf-rock guitar. Los Mirlos: Tiny Desk Concert September 17, 2026 10:00 AM ET Felix Contreras Credit: Photo: Vanessa Castillo/NPR From jazz and Tejano to norteño and ska, 'El Tiny' returns with a takeover from Sept. 15 to Oct. 15 for Latin Music Month . Originally born from Afro-Colombian communities, cumbia spread across the Spanish-speaking world , acquiring distinct musical accents along the way. In Peru, cumbia became particularly popular among oil workers deep in the Amazon. And when Jorge Rodriguez Grández started Los Mirlos in his small hometown of Moyobamba, his band played a regional style called cumbia amazónica, easily identifiable by its electric, reverb-heavy, surf-rock guitar. Sponsor Message Alt.Latino Cumbia: The Musical Backbone Of Latin America Los Mirlos' time behind the Desk is not only a joyful celebration of this music but also a trail of small towns and cities throughout the Amazon jungle. Throughout their performance, these cultural ambassadors share stories and declare their love for cumbia and their tropical homeland. We are so fortunate to host and share with you a group of true pioneers and innovators who, over 50 years later, still effortlessly pump out cumbia grooves. Los Texmaniacs ' music is a living history lesson. The conjunto sound is driven by the button accordion, a mid-19th century instrument that made its way to the U.S.-Mexico border by way of German, Czech and Polish immigrants. But this music is also just perfect for twirling on the dance floor to songs about true love, heartbreak, folk heroes and reflections on life. pages.text: Los Tigres' Tiny Desk, explained : Alt.Latino : NPR Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player Los Tigres' Tiny Desk, explained : Alt.Latino Last week we published a Tiny Desk Concert that ended up being unusual for a few reasons. First of all, it was the final production of our sixth annual El Tiny series. This was a very emotional moment for a lot of reasons. People really love Los Tigres del Norte, to the point that playing their albums feels like sitting with family. And if you’ve seen the introduction I gave the band just before they played at the desk you can see that I wasn’t embarrassed to get emotional when I talked about what the band means to me. That emotional intro led to some changes in our process and format that resulted in a huge response from the audience that went viral. The result was a messy moment behind the scenes here at NPR and more than a little confusion for a lot of you. This week’s episode looks back at last week. First we want to share with you, directly from us, an explanation of what happened. But mostly we want to put the spotlight back on the band and their music because for decades they have been bringing out the kind emotions that got this whole thing started. Give it a listen and enjoy the music. Again. - Felix This podcast episode was produced by Noah Caldwell and edited by Jacob Ganz and Otis Hart. Suraya Mohamed is the executive producer of NPR Music. pages.text: Man with venomous snakes and lizards stopped at German airport Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Man with suitcase full of snakes stopped at German airport 15 October 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Paulin Kola German Customs Not all the the snakes and lizards were alive, officials said A man has been stopped at Cologne Bonn Airport in Germany after trying to smuggle in more than 90 lizards and venomous snakes. Customs officials said the 45-year-old Mexican firefighter had looked "conspicuously nervous" as he tried to go through the green - nothing to declare - exit at the airport. They conducted a drugs test on the man - which came back positive for cocaine - before proceeding to check his suitcase. They did not find any drugs, but vipers, rattlesnakes and other species of snakes and lizards, including iguanas, hidden in shampoo and cream bottles, plastic containers and balls of socks. "My colleagues at the airport are used to a lot when it comes to souvenirs in suitcases, but we've never had 37 live venomous snakes and 55 lizards from Mexico before," said Jens Ahland, spokesman for the Cologne Customs office. Some were being kept "in inhumane conditions", Ahland said. Others had died during the journey from Mexico City via Istanbul. The man, who has not been named, told officers that he had brought the animals back as a favour for a Brazilian acquaintance. He was denied entry to Germany and flown back to Istanbul. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Manatee Awareness Month: Protecting Gentle Giants at the Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse Outstanding Natural Area Nov 3, 2026 Every November, Manatee Awareness Month celebrates one of Florida’s most beloved residents: the West Indian manatee. Often called “sea cows” because of their grazing habits, these gentle giants can grow to more than 10 feet long and weigh over 1,000 pounds. Despite their impressive size, manatees are peaceful, slow-moving animals that spend much of their time feeding on aquatic vegetation, resting, and traveling through coastal waters, rivers, estuaries, and springs. West Indian manatees swim in the clear, shallow waters of the Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse Outstanding Natural Area in Jupiter, Florida. The Bureau of Land Management site is the only BLM-managed area where manatees are regularly observed and provides important habitat for these gentle marine mammals. pages.text: Mary Anning: The forgotten fossil hunter who transformed Britain’s Jurassic Coast | National Geographic HISTORY & CULTURE WOMEN'S HISTORY MONTH The forgotten fossil hunter who transformed Britain’s Jurassic Coast Mary Anning and her most important dinosaur finds went unsung, but her legacy now draws travelers to southwest England. London‘s Natural History Museum displays several of Mary Anning‘s remarkable fossil finds, including this one of an ichthyosaur (lower). Photograph by Tommy Trenchard, Panos Pictures/Redux By Cathy Newman Published March 29, 2021 • 11 min read If you had lived in Victorian times, you’d have spotted her, perhaps, at the foot of Church Cliff to the east of Lyme Regis, a seaside town on England’s southwest coast. She’d have a wicker basket in one hand, a small geologist’s hammer in the other, and be dressed in a plaid coat and cape made of heavy wool—it is chilly by the shore. Her small dog, Tray, would have been skittering by her side. Self-taught paleontologist Mary Anning would search for fossils along the Dorset coast, accompanied by her dog, Tray. Photograph by GL Archive, Alamy Stock Photo What you might not have known then is that Mary Anning was arguably the greatest fossil hunter of them all, “the princess of paleontology,” a contemporary called her. In Victorian England, in an era of amateur scientists, fossil hunters were nearly always men. Anning was born in Lyme Regis, which sits on one of the great fossil deposits from the Jurassic era. WEIRD & WILD Meet 'Hellboy': New Spiky-Headed Dinosaur Found A Triceratops cousin unearthed in Canada is so elaborately adorned "it blows your mind," one paleontologist says. By Devin Powell Published June 4, 2015 • 4 min read Triceratops has a new cousin with a devilishly good nickname: "Hellboy." Paleontologists who excavated the fossil skull of the horned beast from a steep cliff in Canada had a hell of time chipping the 600-pound (270-kilogram) specimen from the hard rock—hence its pet name. Only after freeing the fossil did the crew discover the moniker's pop culture connection. "There are these really stubby horns over the eyes that match up with the comic book character Hellboy ," says study leader Caleb Brown , a paleontologist at the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology in Alberta, Canada. Though it had much smaller horns on its brow than its iconic cousin, the newfound dinosaur boasted a sizable horn on its snout and a fabulous frill on its head. (Also see " New Big-Nosed Horned Dinosaur Found in Utah .") The frill, or bony head protrusion, of Regaliceratops is so elaborate it "blows your mind," one scientist says. pages.text: Meet Marshosaurus, the Jurassic’s Forgotten Predator | National Geographic Marshosaurus considers a Stegosaurus snack at the Natural History Museum of Utah. Photo by Brian Switek. SCIENCE LAELAPS Meet Marshosaurus, the Jurassic’s Forgotten Predator By Riley Black Published November 30, 2015 • 3 min read I’ve spilled more than a little digital ink over the top carnivores of the Jurassic west . Allosaurus , Ceratosaurus , and Torvosaurus are all very dinosaur-y dinosaurs, checking the boxes for big, scary, and strange. But as I’ve poked around the Morrison Formation bones held at the Natural History Museum of Utah over the past few weeks, I realized I’ve done a disservice to ancient ecology by focusing on the flesh-rippers of the most imposing stature. There was an entire guild of Jurassic carnivores running around North America around 150 million years ago, and one of the least-known – at least to the public – is a mid-sized carnivore named Marshosaurus bicentesimus . We know Marshosaurus was part of an wide array of predators, from tiny to giant, because of where it was found. This week's guests remind us not only of the well-documented ways that Cuba revolutionized that gift, but also how it blossomed in South America. Chilean tenor saxophonist Melissa Aldana and Cuban pianist Gonzalo Rubalcaba stopped by after their recent Tiny Desk performance to chat about their own personal histories with jazz and its lineage in their respective countries. The memories Rubalcaba shares about Havana's jazz scene in the 1980s adds another layer to a story we've talked a lot about on Alt.Latino. And Aldana looks back on her youth learning music from her father and grandfather, both of whom were Chilean jazz pioneers. The conversation also covers the music they played at the Tiny Desk, which comes from their recent album, 'Filin,' a reexamination of a Cuban musical movement that lasted from the 1940s through the '60s. Ultimately, this week's episode is time spent with two master musicians to hear how their lives and experiences contribute to their mutual appreciation and love of jazz. pages.text: Mexico drugs: How one DEA killing began a brutal war - BBC News Image caption, The capture and murder of Enrique "Kiki" Camarena was a brazen moment in the drug war By Will Grant BBC News, Guadalajara Twenty seven years ago, the kidnap, torture and murder of a US Drug Enforcement Administration agent by Mexican drug traffickers sparked one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America. It also offered an ominous warning of things to come. The picturesque Mexican city of Guadalajara is bustling with life. By day, its busy plazas are filled with street vendors and shoeshine boys. At night, the mariachis line up to play for the tourists. The country's drug violence feels very far from here and, most of the time, it is. But that was not always the case. "In 1985, Guadalajara was the base of operations for most of the major narcotics traffickers in North America," says James Kuykendall, then-head of the Guadalajara office of the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). "Many of the major traffickers from other parts of Mexico, especially the state of Sinaloa, had migrated to Guadalajara both for the scenery and for the politics: if they didn't have full immunity, certainly no-one was messing with them down there." Among the agents working out of the small office was a 37-year-old Mexican-born American, Enrique "Kiki" Camarena. Most microbiomes contribute to necessary functions within us and our environments, like digestion and plant growth. We are largely living in successful partnership with them. A better understanding of these complex microbial communities would help us harness them for applications to human and animal health, agriculture and food safety, water treatment, manufacturing, renewable energy, and the detection of biological threats. For microbiome research to more quickly deliver products to the clinic and market and make the best use of taxpayer funding, the field requires standardized protocols for sample collection, and reference materials and data. These standardized tools help the many organizations working on microbiome research reproduce each other’s work and build upon it. The microloan program provides loans up to $50,000 to help small businesses and certain not-for-profit childcare centers start up and expand. The average microloan is about $13,000. SBA provides funds to specially designated intermediary lenders, which are nonprofit community-based organizations with experience in lending as well as management and technical assistance. These intermediaries administer the Microloan program for eligible borrowers. Am I eligible? To be eligible for a microloan, businesses must: Not be a type of ineligible business Be an operating business Operate for profit Be located in the U.S. Be small under SBA size requirements How do I use a microloan? I’ve been building Wandering Around , a free browser game in which you can walk around any town or city on Earth. The whole world comes from OpenStreetMap, so I’d like to share how it uses OSM data and ask this community for feedback. Play it here: https://wanderingaround.games (works on phone and desktop, no account needed) News and updates: https://ko-fi.com/wanderingaroundtheworld Screenshots and a short video: https://mikehur.itch.io/wandering-around How the map is built Streets, buildings, water, parks and bridges come from OpenFreeMap vector tiles (zoom 14, OpenMapTiles schema). The game fetches the tiles around the player, decodes them in the browser, stitches buildings that are split across tile edges and turns everything back into OSM-style features with tags. The game logic works on those tags, so it is the same code whether the data comes from tiles or (as a fallback) from Overpass. 2D and 3D: the same data drives a 2D map and a 3D eye-level view. Building heights come from OSM where they are tagged. Transit: train routes and stations, city buses, ferries and signposts come from Overpass queries, so you can travel between real stops and stations. pages.text: Misclassification of Employees as Independent Contractors Under the Fair Labor Standards Act | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Misclassification of Employees as Independent Contractors Under the Fair Labor Standards Act A worker is entitled to minimum wage and overtime pay protections under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) when there is an employment relationship between the worker and an employer and there is coverage under the FLSA. Employers are responsible for determining whether a worker is an employee under the FLSA. Misclassification occurs when an employer treats a worker who is an employee under the FLSA as an independent contractor. Misclassifying employees as independent contractors is a serious problem because misclassified employees may not receive the minimum wage and overtime pay to which they are entitled under the FLSA or other benefits and protections to which they are entitled under the law. As part of its efforts to address misclassification, the Wage and Hour Division on January 10, 2024 published a final rule , effective March 11, 2024, revising its guidance on how to analyze whether a worker is an employee or independent contractor under the FLSA. This guidance is available in the form of regulations at 29 CFR Part 795.
